title: Move slow and make things: What Japanese craftsmanship can teach business about quality, patience, and expertise when AI makes speed cheap
description: AI makes it easier to produce more. The Japanese craft tradition of shokunin offers a guide to making something better.
content: For thirty years, the dominant logic of Western business has been simple: move fast and break things. The first mover has the advantage. Scale before you’re ready. Ship before it’s perfect. Ask forgiveness later. This thinking has produced extraordinary wealth and genuine innovation. It has also created a generation of companies that mistake velocity for value, and are only belatedly discovering that the two are not the same thing. Recommended Video AI has effectively disrupted the disruptors. Speed is now free, which means, for the first time in history, speed is worthless. The ability for anyone to generate strategy, code, or creative work in seconds effectively filled in the moats built on blitzscaling overnight. But this is in fact the opportunity hiding inside the greatest technological acceleration of our lifetimes. AI doesn’t just automate tasks. It clarifies, perhaps for the first time, which human contributions actually matter. It also hands companies a gift few have thought hard about. When machines absorb the administrative and the routine, the defining question becomes what to do with the hours they return. Machines excel at generating the average. Closing the gap between the merely good and the truly extraordinary remains stubbornly, wonderfully human. The Japanese have a word for people who excel at their chosen craft: shokunin. It is often translated as “craftsperson,” but what it really embodies is a quiet competence borne from mastering generations of experience, joined to a sense of pride and a dash of gratitude, both to those who came before and to the materials and people that make the work possible. That combination produces something rare: the taste and skill to deliver quality, along with the humility to admit when change is necessary and the confidence to see a pivot through. There’s a reason some of the planet’s oldest companies can be found in Japan. Nintendo opened its doors in 1889; Shiseido in 1872; the construction firm Kongo Gumi, 578. No, that’s not a typo. These firms revere tradition, but not out of nostalgia. They treat inherited wisdom as something you adapt to changing times so the next generation can flourish, not something you embalm. To a shokunin, the question is not “what can we automate?” It is “what must we never automate?” Every business leader already knows the older version of this rule: never outsource your competitive advantage, never put distance between the company and what makes it special. AI tools are simply the latest way to make that age-old mistake. Firms that know exactly where the line sits hold quiet advantages their competitors cannot purchase or replicate. Shokunin thinking deepens quality, but it also paves the way for innovation. Businesses that rediscover its values will gain what their velocity-chasing competitors cannot buy, borrow, or automate. They will have the confidence to know when something is truly good, and the judgment to pivot when circumstances demand it. AI raises the floor. Shokunin thinking raises the ceiling. Principle 1: Go deep, not wide Constraints look like limitations. Often they are the source of your advantage. Abandon them and you become one of a thousand competitors rather than the only maker of what you make. Just as important, knowing what you do best is what steadies you when conditions turn. In 1921, a small Japanese company called Shimano began making bicycle freewheels in Osaka. Over the following century, as competitors diversified and conglomerates expanded into every adjacent category they could reach, Shimano did something almost perverse in its discipline. It held its ground. The entire portfolio was bicycles and fishing equipment. When opportunities arose to expand into other sporting goods, other mechanical components, other markets entirely, the answer was consistently no. Not yet. Not us. Not that. The result is one of the most quietly dominant competitive positions in modern industry. Today, the majority of the world’s high-performance bicycles ship with Shimano components as standard. The brand rarely advertises. It doesn’t need to. A century of obsessive refinement within a deliberately narrow category produced expertise so deep that competitors who have tried to enter the market found themselves outclassed not by Shimano’s scale, but by the sheer accumulated density of what it knows. That knowledge cannot be acquired in a board meeting or replicated in an accelerator program. It is the product of a hundred years of choosing depth over breadth, every single time the choice was available. Depth also brings something subtler than the courage to pivot. It brings the judgment to know when. Startups famously change course at the first sign of friction, often too quickly. Companies that know exactly what they are can tell a passing squall from a changed climate. Shimano proved it recently. A pandemic-fueled boom in bicycle sales went bust, forcing the company to temporarily shutter its main Japanese factory, while rising e-bike sales threatened its dominance in components for traditional models. But crisis provided opportunity. Shimano used the downtime to develop an AI-driven automatic shifter that analyzes and adapts to a rider’s pedaling habits, letting them climb inclines almost as easily as on an e-bike. A fusion of century-old expertise and cutting-edge technology that no competitor can replicate, because no competitor has the century. It is also a preview of the choice every company will soon face. When automation hands back the hours once consumed by routine, you can use them to produce more, or to get better. Shimano chose better. The key insight: Master one thing completely and you will never be lost when the world turns. Depth is what makes reinvention possible. Principle 2: Taste is a skill Americans invented blue jeans. But the Japanese arguably perfected them. Introduced by American occupation forces after World War II, jeans found a market among young Japanese eager to emulate Hollywood stars. Within a few decades, local makers had gone from importing American fabric to producing their own, and by the Eighties they had grown so adept that even Levi’s began experimenting with denim made in Japan. The twist was that Japanese denim-spinners weren’t mimicking the denims of the Eighties. They were intent on taking things back to the Fifties. By any objective standard, that technology was outdated, labor-intensive, imprecise, and inefficient. American makers had long since moved on. The older spinning methods produced yarn riddled with faults that surfaced as the indigo faded, as denim expert Andrew Olah explained to W. David Marx in the book Ametora: How Japan Saved American Fashion. Where American makers saw a defect, the Japanese saw the main feature of the product. They wanted to capture a vibe. “It’s easy to make jeans exactly like vintage,” explained Hidehiko Yamane, founder of Evisu Jeans. “Anyone can do that.” Rather, he wanted to offer the feeling of seeing America through Japanese eyes. With his partner Mikiharu Tsujita, he disassembled vintage jeans, studying every swatch and stitch to learn why they felt so much better than modern wear. The answer lay in selvedge, a denim woven on old-fashioned shuttle looms that Western manufacturers had long abandoned for being too slow. A handful of mills in rural Okayama still ran them, and agreed to work to the partners’ exacting specifications. Initially the company produced just fourteen pairs a day, hand-painting the signature seagull logo on each pocket. By the turn of the millennium, tastemakers like David Beckham, Jay-Z, and Beyoncé were flaunting Evisu, sparking a wave of interest in Japanese brands that continues to the present day. Selvedge is now synonymous with premium denim worldwide, and the mills of Okayama supply fabric to high-end jeans makers far beyond Japan, for garments selling at hundreds, even thousands of dollars.
